title: Packet capture with tcpdump, and ARP/neighbour inspection
summary: Capture is the ground truth when arguments about 'whose fault it is' go nowhere. This lesson covers safe, narrow captures and how to read neighbour tables.

sections.heading: Safe capturing rules
sections.html:
Packet capture sees every packet on the interface, which means private network details, hostnames, session tokens and sometimes credentials in cleartext protocols. Follow these rules:

  • Always bound the capture: -c N for a packet count, -w file to a file rather than a flooding terminal, and a narrow -i interface.
  • Always filter: host, port, net. Never capture an unfiltered stream on a busy link.
  • Redact before sharing: strip MACs, IPs and payloads before pasting into a ticket. Mention that you did.
  • Permissions: tcpdump needs root or CAP_NET_RAW; put the user in a group or use a capability rather than running your whole investigation as root.

sections.heading: The filters you will actually use
sections.html:
# DHCP conversation, boundedsudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n -c 40 'port 67 or port 68'
# DNS queries to and from one hostsudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n -c 20 'udp port 53 and host 10.0.0.53'
# TCP handshake to a servicesudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n -c 20 'tcp port 443 and host 203.0.113.20'
# ARP only (is the gateway answering?)sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n -e -c 20 arp
# full packets, no payload truncation, to a filesudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n -w /tmp/nq.pcap 'host 10.0.0.5 and tcp port 22'

Flag reference: -n no name resolution (faster, avoids extra DNS), -nn no port names either, -e show link-layer headers, -A ASCII payload, -X hex+ASCII, -s 0 full packet, -w write pcap.

sections.heading: Reading a capture
sections.html:
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n -c 6 'tcp port 443 and host 203.0.113.20'12:04:11.104231 IP 10.20.30.44.51234 > 203.0.113.20.443: Flags [S], seq 1, win 64240, options [mss 1460]
12:04:11.112004 IP 203.0.113.20.443 > 10.20.30.44.51234: Flags [S.], seq 2, ack 2, win 65160
12:04:11.112233 IP 10.20.30.44.51234 > 203.0.113.20.443: Flags [.], ack 2
12:04:11.140881 IP 10.20.30.44.51234 > 203.0.113.20.443: Flags [P.], seq 2:518, ack 2  # TLS ClientHello
12:04:11.160002 IP 203.0.113.20.443 > 10.20.30.44.51234: Flags [P.], seq 2:1430, ack 518
12:04:11.161120 IP 10.20.30.44.51234 > 203.0.113.20.443: Flags [.], ack 1430

What the flags tell you:

PatternMeaning
S then S. then .Successful three-way handshake
S repeated with no replyPackets leaving, nothing returning — DROP, routing or dead host
S then RRefused: port closed or REJECT rule
S then ICMP unreachableNo route, or an administrative block
R mid-sessionSomething killed the connection (firewall state, app crash, RST injection)
Retransmissions of the same seqLoss on one direction of the path

This table is the single most useful diagnostic artefact in this module: it turns 'the network is broken' into a specific, localised finding.

sections.heading: ARP and the neighbour table
sections.html:
IPv4 ARP (and IPv6 NDP) resolve an on-link address to a link-layer address. The results live in the neighbour table:

$ ip neigh show10.20.30.1 dev eth0 lladdr 52:54:00:aa:bb:01 REACHABLE
10.20.30.99 dev eth0 lladdr 52:54:00:cc:dd:02 STALE
10.20.31.7 dev eth0  FAILED
StateMeaning
REACHABLERecently confirmed; usable
STALEKnown but unverified; a packet triggers revalidation
DELAY / PROBEUnicast revalidation in progress
INCOMPLETERequest sent, no reply yet
FAILEDDid not resolve; traffic to it is dropped
PERMANENTStatically configured, never expires

A FAILED or INCOMPLETE entry for the default gateway is one of the most useful findings in networking: it proves the L2 problem is local and that nothing beyond the host matters yet. Clearing entries to force re-resolution: sudo ip neigh flush dev eth0 (careful on production systems — it briefly interrupts traffic).

sections.heading: Gratuitous ARP and why it matters
sections.html: A host may send an ARP announcement (gratuitous ARP) when an interface comes up or an address moves — for example a floating IP on an HA pair. Switches and hosts update their tables from it, which is what makes failover fast. It is also how ARP spoofing works, which is why dynamic ARP inspection exists on managed switches.

checks.prompt: A capture shows repeated SYN packets from the client to 203.0.113.20:443 with no responses. What does this prove?
options: The SYN leaves the client but no response returns — the cause is downstream (filter, route, or host)
checks.explanation: You can only conclude that packets leave and nothing comes back. That localises the fault to the path or the server, but does not yet say which.

why_wrong.3: A down application usually yields RST (refused), not silence.
why_wrong.1: The capture shows the client already has the IP address.
why_wrong.2: A failing NIC would not produce a clean SYN sequence.

checks.prompt: `ip neigh` shows the default gateway in state FAILED. What is the most useful next step?
options: Run dig against an external resolver
Check link state and ARP reachability on the local segment — the failure is local
checks.explanation: A FAILED neighbour entry means no ARP reply from the gateway. The problem is on the local link: cable, VLAN, port, or the gateway itself.

why_wrong.2: DNS needs the gateway resolved first.
why_wrong.0: External DNS is unreachable without a working gateway.

connect.title: Switching
connect.text: ARP broadcasts are what the switch floods; the neighbour table is the result of that flooding.

connect.title: TCP states
connect.text: The capture's flag sequence maps directly onto ss states: SYN-SENT, ESTAB, FIN-WAIT.

connect.title: Case studies 4 and 12
connect.text: Both hinge on distinguishing a silent drop from an active refusal.

interview.q: How would you prove whether packets are leaving the host at all?
interview.a: Capture on the host's interface with a narrow filter. If SYNs appear but no responses return, the host is transmitting and the problem is downstream. If nothing appears, the problem is local: application, routing, or a wrong destination address.

interview.q: What is a neighbour table and what does FAILED mean?
interview.a: The ARP/NDP cache mapping IP addresses to MAC addresses on the local segment. FAILED means resolution was attempted and no reply arrived, so the kernel drops traffic to that address — a definite local Layer 2 problem.
